How this list is ordered

Four gates, applied in this order to every published US record. There is no score and no weighting — each gate either separates two machines or hands them to the next one.

  1. 1 Does it run the set?

    Every record is put through the compatibility engine against all of the loads at once — running watts against continuous output, the worst start-up instant against the surge ceiling, waveform where a load demands one. Green first, then the tight fits, then anything the engine could not read, then the machines that cannot do it. A machine that cannot start the load in front of it is not a cheaper option.

  2. 2 Can we prove how long?

    A runtime is only printed where the brand publishes what it takes to compute one — depth of discharge and inverter efficiency — and never from the number on the box. Records that reach the target sort first, records with a proven but shorter figure next (longest first: inside that band none of them does the job, so the one that gets closest wins), and records whose duration cannot be proven at all sort last inside their verdict band. That is a statement about published data, not about the hardware, and each of those rows says so.

  3. 3 Can it be bought today?

    A record under a verified out-of-stock policy, or one we may not sell into your state, sorts behind an equivalent one that can be bought. It stays on the list with the reason attached rather than disappearing.

  4. 4 Then price.

    Cheapest first, inside everything above. One mains standard and one currency per page, so every comparison is like for like. A record with no verified price sorts to the back of its own band — the absence of a price is not a low price.

One inrush figure is reported and never enforced

A switching power supply charges its input capacitors the instant it is plugged in, and that spike can be large — but it lasts a few line cycles, two orders of magnitude shorter than the second-scale event a station’s surge rating describes. The two are not the same quantity, so this site reports the figure and never fails a verdict on it. It is not in the start-up total above, and that is not an omission.

Applies to: Laptop computer

Some loads publish no start-up figure at all

Nobody publishes an inrush figure for these, and this library does not invent one. They are electronics rather than motors, so there is no rotor to break free and no reason to expect one; the engine says so rather than assuming a number in either direction.

Applies to: LED light bulb

Why 9 records rank below machines they out-spec

9 of the 12 records here start and hold this load set and still rank below machines they out-spec, for one reason: EcoFlow and Jackery publish no depth of discharge and no inverter efficiency for them, so the hours a reader actually wants cannot be computed from anything but the number on the box — and dividing a nameplate by a load is the one thing this site will not do. The other side of that is BLUETTI: it is the only brand here that publishes both, which is the whole reason every proven runtime above belongs to it. The rule rewarded disclosure, not hardware.

What their rows do carry is the bound: that record’s nameplate over this set’s average draw of 159 W, which is arithmetic anyone can redo against the summary above — floored, never rounded up, so the printed ceiling never claims an hour more than the number supports — and it is printed on every one of those rows. But it is a ceiling and not a duration: it assumes the pack surrenders every watt-hour printed on it and that the inverter loses nothing turning DC into AC, and no battery does either. The real hours sit somewhere below that ceiling, and the two missing figures are exactly what would say how far below. That is the difference between a number this page will print and a number it will not.

The scope of that finding, stated: as of 2026-08-01 we read each manufacturer’s own published documents for these 9 models and found no depth-of-discharge and no inverter-efficiency figure in them. It is a statement about what those documents contained on that date — not a claim that the number exists nowhere. Send us one that is published and the record moves, and the row moves with it. This is a statement about published data, not about the hardware — the verdict column judges that separately, and it comes first.

The load that changes the answer

Add a portable induction cooktop to the same set and the first gate, which was already turning records away, tightens further: not one of the 12 clears it outright — 1 is a tight fit and 11 cannot do it at all. Cooking on induction is the decision that changes almost every answer on this list, the same way adding a room air conditioner does for a house — it is worth making before you choose the machine rather than after. The quiz carries this set as a preset.

Questions people ask about this list

How many of the 12 actually run it?
11 of 12 do, and the other 1 is the finding on this page. 194 W of running draw and 249 W at the worst start-up instant is what every published US record is measured against, and 1 of 12 runs out of ceiling somewhere in it. Which means the buying question splits in two: whether a given machine starts it at all, and only then how long it holds. The rows below answer them in that order. Add a portable induction cooktop to the same set and the first gate, which was already turning records away, tightens further: not one of the 12 clears it outright — 1 is a tight fit and 11 cannot do it at all. Cooking on induction is the decision that changes almost every answer on this list, the same way adding a room air conditioner does for a house — it is worth making before you choose the machine rather than after. The quiz carries this set as a preset.
Why is the biggest machine not first?
Because this page ranks by what can be proven about the question it asks. Capacity only counts once a brand publishes what it takes to turn that capacity into hours — depth of discharge and inverter efficiency. 9 of the 12 records here publish neither — the same count the panel above prints as unprovable, and each of those rows says which two figures are missing. Every one of them starts and holds this set and still ranks below a machine it out-specs. Nothing about their electrical performance is being marked down: the verdict column judges that separately, and it comes first.
What is actually being tested here?
194 W of running draw and 249 W at the worst start-up instant, put through the compatibility engine against each machine's continuous output, surge ceiling and inverter waveform. A load above 82% of continuous output drops out of the green whatever else is true. The itemised set, with each figure's source and date, is at the top of this page.
How current are the prices?
Every price on this page carries the date it was last checked, next to the figure. Past fourteen days the page says how old it is rather than showing it as current. Prices move; the ranking above them is recomputed on every build from the same records.
Is this list paid for?
No. Nothing on this page can be bought into: the order is the four-gate rule printed above the list, applied to every published record in this region. The one buy link on this page goes to the record the rule selected.
